records.sourceFile: The Effectiveness of    Photobiomodulation Therapy Versus Cryotherapy for Skeletal Muscle   Recovery-  A Critically Appraised Topic.pdf

paper.citation: Fisher SR, Rigby JH, Mettler JA, McCurdy KW. The Effectiveness of Photobiomodulation Therapy Versus Cryotherapy for Skeletal Muscle Recovery: A Critically Appraised Topic. J Sport Rehabil. 2019;28(5):526-531.
paper.abstract: Critically appraised topic of five studies comparing photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) with cryotherapy for muscle recovery after strenuous exercise. All five favoured PBMT, and the authors rate the evidence as grade B.
paper.tldr: After hard exercise, photobiomodulation looked better than cryotherapy for muscle damage markers, soreness and muscle performance in this appraisal. The human evidence is three small trials, so treat PBMT as a promising option rather than a settled replacement for cryotherapy.
paper.methods: The authors searched MEDLINE and SPORTDiscus and hand-searched reference lists for studies of level 2 evidence or higher that directly compared PBMT with cryotherapy after exercise. Five studies met the criteria, and the three human trials were scored on the PEDro scale (scores of 7 to 9).
paper.findings: In the human trials, PBMT improved strength (maximal voluntary contraction) recovery and reduced soreness and creatine kinase relative to placebo over roughly 24 to 96 hours, while cryotherapy alone was not different from placebo, which the authors read as PBMT outperforming cryotherapy. In the futsal trial, LED therapy lowered creatine kinase and blood lactate from post-exercise values but peak and mean Wingate power did not differ between groups. In the rat studies, LED therapy produced less muscle damage and inflammation than cold-water immersion or passive recovery.
paper.limitations: Two of the five studies are rat studies, so their results do not transfer directly to humans, and the authors call for more unbiased in vivo human research. Most human comparisons were each treatment against placebo rather than direct PBMT versus cryotherapy tests. All studies used low-powered PBMT devices, and treatment parameters varied, which the authors say may affect outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest PBMT can be considered in place of cryotherapy after exercise for muscle recovery, with the main gains in soreness and performance recovery. They also note that cryotherapy showed little benefit over placebo in these studies, and that more human research is needed before firm clinical recommendations.
paper.athleteDev: The evidence concerns recovery between training or competition bouts, where PBMT was linked to faster return of muscle torque and lower soreness than placebo, while cryotherapy was not. It does not show that PBMT improves performance during a session, and the human samples were untrained men, men of unstated training status, or six professional futsal players.
paper.rtp: The studies measured muscle damage, soreness and torque after exercise bouts rather than after injury, so this appraisal cannot inform rehabilitation or return to sport.

records.sourceFile: The Influence of Post-Exercise        Cold-Water Immersion on Adaptive Responses to Exercise- A Review of   the      Literature.pdf

paper.citation: Broatch JR, Petersen A, Bishop DJ. The Influence of Post-Exercise Cold-Water Immersion on Adaptive Responses to Exercise: A Review of the Literature. Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: Post-exercise cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used to reduce fatigue and speed recovery between sessions, but reports suggest it may attenuate long-term adaptations. This review examines the molecular mechanisms by which CWI may alter signalling and adaptation in human skeletal muscle, focusing on mitochondrial biogenesis and muscle protein turnover. Single sessions of CWI may increase markers of mitochondrial biogenesis in the short term, but regular CWI has little to no effect on endurance adaptations, and evidence for resistance training suggests either no effect or a negative effect on strength and muscle mass.
paper.tldr: Cold-water immersion after exercise can raise short-term markers of mitochondrial biogenesis, but regular use has little effect on endurance adaptations and may blunt strength and muscle gains after resistance training. There is no adaptation-based reason to add routine CWI, and some reason for caution in strength or hypertrophy blocks.
paper.methods: Narrative review. A Scopus search using the keywords cold, skeletal muscle and exercise covered abstracts from 1963 to December 2017, and reference lists of included articles were searched. Articles were included if they addressed molecular mechanisms by which cold given during or after exercise alters skeletal muscle responses, including intracellular signalling, gene transcription and protein translation related to mitochondrial biogenesis and protein turnover.
paper.findings: After a single endurance session, CWI increased PGC-1a mRNA in the cooled limb (up to about 9-fold), but two studies found no change in PGC-1a protein content up to 3 hours after exercise. Regular CWI during endurance training (3 to 6 weeks) had negligible or slightly beneficial effects on cycling performance in several studies, while one study using colder immersion (5 degrees C) found attenuated endurance and maximal oxygen uptake. Regular CWI during resistance training attenuated strength and muscle mass gains in some studies (including Roberts et al., 21 men, 12 weeks), but had no detrimental effect in others.
paper.limitations: Many included studies immersed only one limb, used a single exercise or lower-body training only, and trained at 2 to 3 sessions per week, below the load of many athletes. Results differ between studies with similar protocols, and the authors note that some proposed mechanisms are speculative and unverified. Some cited molecular work is limited to small human samples and animal models, and the review was not systematic.
paper.practicalImplications: Where the goal is endurance mitochondrial adaptation, the review gives no reason to add CWI to training. Where the goal is strength or muscle mass after resistance training, it gives no reason to add CWI and some reason for caution. Whether CWI changes adaptation when recovery between closely spaced sessions is limited has not been tested, so the review cannot settle that case.
paper.athleteDev: Avoid making cold immersion a routine after every strength session, since some studies show blunted strength or muscle gains. The review found no study showing that regular CWI improves strength or muscle mass, and no conclusive evidence that it increases mitochondrial content or function.
paper.rtp: It does not address return to sport or rehabilitation. The studies concern healthy exercisers' training adaptations; the review's background statement that CWI may reduce soft-tissue injury effects is not tested by the included evidence, so it cannot guide rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.
